set.overview: Red Mountain is a Class 2 tundra-and-talus ridge walk that links to Culebra Peak, so nearly everyone climbs Culebra first and then continues south to this 13,911-foot summit. It lies entirely on private ranch land in the Sangre de Cristo Range and can only be climbed on a booked, paid outing that starts at the ranch headquarters. The link has no exposure and simple routefinding, though it is a real workout after the Culebra climb.
set.approach: Check in at the ranch headquarters, then drive the ranch's 4WD road to the four-way junction about 3.4 miles in, at roughly 11,200 feet, where there is plenty of parking. The upper trailhead sits a mile farther, near 11,650 feet, when the ranch allows driving to it. From the junction, walk east about a mile to the road end beside a small stream, cross it, and follow the drainage to a saddle on Culebra's northwest ridge. Take that ridge to the Culebra summit; the Red Mountain climb starts from there.
set.descent_text: From the summit, retrace the same line north over the saddles to Culebra Peak, then go back down Culebra's northwest ridge to the stream and the road end. Contouring below Culebra's summit to skip the regain saves little effort and tends to cause foot problems, so most parties simply cross over the top again.
hazards: Private land: the only legal access is the booked ranch outing, and trespassers are prosecuted
Everyone must be signed out by 6 pm; a late return can bring a search response and a donation request
Culebra's northwest ridge, which you cross both ways, has a couple of rough sections
Loose rubble and talus on the final 300 feet to the summit

review.notes: Season Jan-Jul: one page says no climbing Aug 1 through December, winter outings start in January; the other says January through July in recent years. Ranch policy changes; Friday-Sunday only. Gain and distance SKIPPED: the only figure (8.2 mi / 4,070 ft) is for Culebra plus Red from the four-way, i.e. includes a second peak.

set.overview: The Southeast Ridge is the standard Class 2+ way up 13,909-foot Vermilion Peak in the San Juan Mountains above Telluride. It is normally reached by working along the crest from Fuller Peak, over a loose, rubbly ridge with a short, crumbly scramble just below the summit. The terrain is all rubble, scree and talus with little exposure, but a tower midway along the traverse takes some care to get around.
set.approach: Start at the Lake Hope trailhead, about 10,745 feet, reached from Telluride via State Highway 145, County Road 63A and then forest road 627. The last couple of miles of that road are rough and call for high clearance. From the lake the route climbs in sequence over the ridge points toward Beattie and then Fuller Peak; from Fuller it is roughly 0.6 mile and 400 feet of climbing along the crest to Vermilion.
set.descent_text: Go back along the ridge to the saddle between Vermilion and Fuller, then continue the traverse to the saddle with Golden Horn by way of the rubble bench beneath the northeast face cliffs. Dropping straight down the ridge toward Golden Horn is steep and seldom done.
hazards: Loose rubble and a short crumbly scramble just below the summit
A tower partway along the Fuller-to-Vermilion traverse that takes care to get around
A notch with brief exposure and loose rock on the ridge sections earlier in the sequence
Rubble and talus throughout; an ice axe is advised if snow lingers

review.notes: Single source for all text. Distance SKIPPED: the only figures (9.15 mi round trip, ~4,450 ft) include Beattie and Fuller. Season SKIPPED: only a club trip window found, not a route statement. gain_ft already stored (3809) left alone.

set.overview: Casco Peak's north ridge is a Class 2+ route to a 13,905-foot Sawatch summit, usually done as part of a day with Frasco Benchmark and French Mountain. The ridge crest crosses several rock ribs and a high point before a tundra slope leads to a final stretch of slabs, ledges and boulders. Optional third-class scrambling is available but not required.
set.approach: Begin at the South Halfmoon Creek trailhead, around 10,290 feet, up a long gravel road from Leadville; the final stretch toward the creek crossing is rated 4WD and many vehicles stop short, so expect to park along the creek and walk. The creek is crossed about 1.1 miles in, and the hike then runs roughly 3.6 miles to near 11,725 feet, working around willows in the basin before climbing toward the ridge.
set.descent_text: Come down Casco's southeast ridge, which is easier ground, to about 13,200 feet. There, leave the ridge heading east-northeast into the South Halfmoon basin and pick up the old road, which is simple to find. Early in the season a glissade may be possible, so carry an ice axe.
hazards: Lightning and strong wind on the exposed ridge
Glissading slushy snow has caused a serious injury here; use caution on early-season snow
The Halfmoon Creek crossing can be dangerous at runoff-level water
Willows in the basin and loose stacked boulders slow travel

review.notes: Single source. Gain and distance SKIPPED: published figures (11.85 mi / 4,555 ft) are for the combined outing over Frasco and French. Season not stated by any page I opened.

set.overview: A remote Class 2 walk to the 13,904-foot summit of Phoenix Peak in the La Garita Mountains above Creede. It follows a stock-driveway trail, then open tundra slopes, to a saddle south of the top and finishes over rubble to the high point. Exposure is nil, but the faint trail in places and the length make it a long day.
set.approach: From Creede go north on the gravel road that becomes County Road 503, stay right at the fork about 1.2 miles out onto CR 502, and follow East Willow Creek. A passenger car can reach the first switchback; a good-clearance 4WD can continue to the upper trailhead near 10,340 feet. From there the trail crosses Whited Creek and climbs the open slope beyond, then follows the La Garita Stock Driveway trail south and east up a side drainage, crossing the stream several times and relying on cairns where the tread fades. Timberline is near 10,750 feet.
set.descent_text: Retrace the ascent: down the rubble to the saddle, down the narrow ridge and the tundra slopes to the drainage, then along the stock driveway trail back to the upper trailhead. Stopping at the lower switchback adds roughly three miles round trip.
hazards: Faint, cairned trail in the side drainage makes routefinding moderate
The footbridge near the start may be gone, leaving a wet crossing
Rubble and talus on the upper slopes
Long day if the rough road cannot be driven

evidence.fact: 9.4 mi round trip, 3,585 ft gain from the upper East Willow Creek 4WD trailhead (10,340 ft)
9.4 mi round trip stated; halved to 4.7 mi one way = 7.56 km

review.notes: Single source; measured from the upper 4WD trailhead, so a passenger-car start is longer. Summit minus trailhead = 3,564 ft, gain is consistent. Season not stated.

set.overview: The Stemwinder is a 1936 route of about six pitches and roughly 1,000 feet up the right side of Thor Peak's big south face above Whitney Portal. It is easy fifth class, rated 5.4, with a short awkward chimney near the start, steep chimneys mixed with class 3 and 4 scrambling, an exposed slab pitch, and a final traverse before talus leads to the summit. A light alpine rack is enough.
set.approach: Follow the main Whitney Trail from the Portal and leave it near Bighorn Park, before the signs for Lone Pine Lake. Go cross-country up and to the right through forest and slabs to the base of the south face; allow about an hour and a half to two hours. A 10-foot class 3 to 4 chimney leads to the first pitch. Access to the upper parts of the Lone Pine Creek watershed is limited from May to October, so check current Whitney Zone rules.
set.descent_text: The line used for the descent goes down the northeast slope into the North Fork of Lone Pine Creek, carrying all gear since the climb does not return to the base. A shorter way off the south face may exist but is not documented.
hazards: Hard first move into the crux chimney that feels harder than the grade
Poor rock in the steep fourth-class chimney
Very exposed slab moves and an exposed traverse near the top
Little protection beyond a few fixed pitons, so a light rack and careful footwork matter

review.notes: Gain and distance SKIPPED: only a trip blog states 7 mi / 4,000 ft with no clear scope. Season SKIPPED. Descent is from one report.

hazards: Rock is often crumbly, though the hard sections are short
No water on the ridge; the descent may have some depending on the time of year
The east-ledges descent has no trail or cairns, the ridgeline forks repeatedly, and steep cliffs lie to the south and southeast
The descent gully is loose and shrubby; a shortcut to a nearer gully can involve a short class 5 chimney
